extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (particularly those writing ensemble casts)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for making each member of an ensemble cast distinct and identifiable through goals, motivation, physicality, and especially voice so dialogue and actions read as belonging to the right character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with the protagonist
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with the protagonist protagonist and build a spiderweb of how the other characters interact with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the protagonist as the hub for relationships and contrasts; map interactions to discover how ensemble members relate to the central figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared goal plus individual goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Every member of your ensemble has a reason to be there; make sure every single character wants their own thing that is separate from the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give characters both the group's shared objective (e.g., 'destroy the Death Star') and distinct personal goals so they act and respond differently; thinking about 'what they want' reveals personality and drives decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation as a primary distinguishing tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Motivation is a great place to start — each character should have specific things they want, which informs how they behave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrow from role-playing/group dynamics: different players/characters have different reasons for being present (escape, companionship, power), which creates vibrancy; avoid flat motivation where everyone wants the same thing for the same reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must be trying to do different things
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure they each have their own goal, that they are really trying to do something that is different from what everyone else is interested in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict and contrast arise when ensemble members pursue divergent goals; this creates interesting interactions and highlights distinctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice (how they talk) matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Spend time thinking about voice — what does this character sound like? Their singular voice makes them who they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think and 'be' the character to hear their voice; voice should be consistent and distinct enough that lines feel native to that character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give the right person the right lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure the right person has the right lines — jokes or well-worded lines must go to someone who can deliver them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a joke or line is out-of-character for the speaker, it will knock the reader out of the story; you may need to bend plot or reassign lines so the person on stage matches the line's tone and vocabulary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid out-of-character dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: A fantastic line of dialogue that’s out of character for someone will knock the reader out of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revision should check that dialogue fits the character's vocabulary, mood, and abilities; if not, rewrite the line or give it to a different character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct vs. unique (the silhouette test)
rubrics_metrics.description: You don’t need every character to be unique; you need them to be distinct — the reader must be able to tell them apart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even identical twins who look similar can be made distinct via voice, catchphrases, recurring behaviors; aim for recognizable differences rather than forcing arbitrary uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catchphrases and recurring verbal ticks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use things that only a particular character will say (a catchphrase) so that you don't need dialogue tags to identify the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A repeated line or verbal pattern helps readers instantly identify the speaker; use sparingly and appropriately so it remains recognizable without becoming gimmicky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical features and outer distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical features, distinctive clothing, or other outward signs can help readers identify characters at a glance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use one or two strong visual markers (e.g., jean jacket with buttons) rather than loading every character with too many flashy details, which makes distinctions meaningless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner distinctions: distinct problems and behavior patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Give each character an inner distinction such as a distinct problem or predictable emotional response (e.g., 'Ryan is the angry one').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inner traits guide plausible reactions to situations and make ensemble dynamics readable; combine inner and outer markers for quick recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'everything and the kitchen sink' design
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t overload characters with too many distinctive trappings—too many cool things makes everyone blend together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist the impulse to give every character extreme visual or quirky items; targeted, meaningful details are more effective for distinctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: POV selection: pick the most interesting/painful POV wisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on the character who is in the most pain as a way to pick the most interesting POV, but be careful not to pull focus away from the ensemble members for that book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a side character offers a more painful or interesting POV, weigh whether using them will undermine the ensemble focus; rotating POVs is okay but ensure ensemble cohesion and characterization get preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match line-level diction to character
rubrics_metrics.description: Change lines to fit who’s speaking — what seems poetic for one character may be wrong for another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you draft a great sentence, test it in-character; if it doesn't fit, rewrite it multiple times or assign it to a different character whose voice matches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make descriptions by POV character distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: If writing in first person, the narrator's description of other ensemble members must reflect that narrator's voice and viewpoint so each supporting character sounds different through the narrator's lens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-person narration should still convey distinct voices for other characters via the narrator's unique descriptors; ensure the narrator's perspective doesn't flatten ensemble members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ensemble dynamics to highlight differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Design scenes and plots that intentionally highlight how different characters interact with the central issue, letting each 'bounce off' it in unique ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sitcoms and ensemble TV (Community, Seinfeld, Friends, Defenders) are cited examples — structure scenes to show varied reactions and beliefs to make contrasts clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test voice perception via role-play/mirroring exercises (homework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical exercise: have each of your ensemble characters describe themselves, then have each describe each of the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This matrix (N characters → N^2 descriptions) reveals how voice affects perception and helps you see whether characters are distinct; do mirror scenes and short exercises even if you won't put them in the book.
